# MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation

Kayshav Bhardwaj Affiliation: Purdue University
Email: [bhardw43@purdue.edu](mailto:)    Pragun Seth Affiliation: UC
Berkeley Email: [pragunseth@berkeley.edu](mailto:)    Kush Bhardwaj
Affiliation: University of Illinois
Email: [kushb2@illinois.edu](mailto:)    Vijay Nagasamy Affiliation: UC
Berkeley Email: [vjnagasamy@gmail.com](mailto:)    Kurt Keutzer
Affiliation: UC Berkeley Email: [keutzer@berkeley.edu](mailto:)

###### Abstract

Classical Sanskrit poses three linguistic challenges monolithic
foundation models do not resolve in one generation call: morphophonemic
fusion (Sandhi), dense nominal compounding (Samāsa), and discourse-level
zero-anaphora forced by poetic meter. We present MITRA-Swarm, a
multi-agent architecture injecting explicit linguistic structure into an
otherwise monolithic pipeline: a Sandhi-splitting agent, a parallel
array of generalist (gemma-4-26B-A4B-it) and domain-specialized
(gemma-2-mitra-it) translators, and a discourse-aware Ellipsis Restorer
that consults corpus-derived register tags to avoid inventing
active-voice subjects in impersonal legal and philosophical registers.
Quality is estimated by two strictly separated judges: a routing judge
($`J_{\text{route}}`$, same model family as the generators) driving an
internal critique loop, and an independent reporting judge
($`J_{\text{report}}=`$gpt-4o-mini, no shared vendor lineage) scoring
every output exactly once. On a stratified benchmark of 1,000 verses
across five registers (23,990 scored verdicts, 12-condition
pre-registered ablation), the full swarm reaches $`85.90`$ MQM against a
monolithic baseline of $`85.27`$ ($`\Delta=+0.63`$,
$`p_{\text{adj}}=0.0018`$, 95% CI $`[+0.30,+0.97]`$), and isolated
discourse restoration alone accounts for $`+0.44`$ MQM
($`p_{\text{adj}}=0.0288`$), outperforming a call-count-matched
self-refinement baseline by $`+0.51`$ MQM ($`p_{\text{adj}}=0.0288`$).
Severe per-verse failures (MQM $`<80`$) fall from $`9.0\%`$ to
$`7.6\%`$, at roughly $`9\times`$ the per-verse inference cost of the
baseline. Beyond these headline effects, we report two findings about
evaluation itself: $`J_{\text{route}}`$ scores its own family’s outputs
$`2`$–$`7`$ MQM higher than $`J_{\text{report}}`$ on every one of the 12
conditions, empirically motivating the two-judge split; and a preflight
screen of a 192,151-entry retrieval index against all 12 evaluation
works verifies 0 reference leaks across 269 runtime checks. We report
these as small effects on a metric that saturates near 85-86 across
every condition.

## 1 Introduction

Sanskrit is the primary linguistic repository for a vast corpus of
classical Indian philosophy, science, and literature, yet remains
severely under-resourced in modern NLP: the lack of large parallel
corpora and the language’s grammatical complexity have historically
limited MT quality ([Haddow et al., 2022](#bib.bib12); [Costa-jussà et
al., 2022](#bib.bib15)). Foundation models trained overwhelmingly on
high-resource, concatenative languages do not, by default, carry the
inductive biases classical Sanskrit requires, i.e. no mechanism for
undoing phonetic fusion at word boundaries, no structured representation
of deeply nested compounds, and no discourse memory built to restore an
argument elided clauses earlier for metrical reasons, which in turn
produces translations marred by omission, semantic drift, and
hallucination ([Ji et al., 2023](#bib.bib21)).

Three linguistic properties make this failure systematic rather than
incidental:

- •
  Sandhi (Morphophonemic Fusion): phonetic mergers at word boundaries
  obscure lexical boundaries without pre-translation segmentation,
  causing out-of-vocabulary and dictionary-lookup failures.
- •
  Samāsa (Nominal Compounding): compounds, sometimes spanning entire
  clauses, leave the syntactic and semantic relations between their
  constituents implicit.
- •
  High Ellipsis (Zero Anaphora): metrical verse systematically omits
  subjects, objects, even verbs, requiring inference from the
  surrounding discourse.

A monolithic model attempts segmentation, reordering, lexical
translation, and discourse-level argument restoration in a single
generation call; without explicit modular guidance it loses local
morphosemantic structure, hallucinates relations between compound
members, and invents target-language arguments rather than interrogating
the source. MITRA-Swarm instead injects each linguistic principle as an
explicit, separately-verifiable pipeline stage:

1.  1.  A morphological Sandhi Parser decomposes phonetic mergers and
        compounds into a structured morphosemantic guide before translation.
2.  2.  A parallel generator array of a generalist frontier model
        (gemma-4-26B-A4B-it) and a domain-specialized fine-tune
        (gemma-2-mitra-it) compares specialization against raw scale rather
        than assuming it.
3.  3.  A discourse-level Ellipsis Restorer with register-aware voice
        guarding
        (Section [3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Ellipsis and Zero-Anaphora Argument Restoration with Register-Aware Voice Guarding ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation"))
        restores zero-anaphora referents in narrative registers while
        suppressing invented active-voice subjects in impersonal legal
        (Dharmaśāstra) and philosophical (Sūtra) injunctions.
4.  4.  A two-judge quality architecture: a routing judge
        $`J_{\text{route}}`$ (shares a model family with the generators)
        drives an internal critique loop; an independent reporting judge
        $`J_{\text{report}}`$ (shares no vendor lineage with any generator
        or $`J_{\text{route}}`$) scores every finished output exactly once,
        off the critical path, for the numbers in this paper.

When $`J_{\text{route}}`$’s estimate falls below threshold, a Critique
Agent diagnoses errors, a Tool Selector queries whatever retrieval tools
are genuinely backed by data, and a Refinement Agent rewrites the
translation.

Our contributions:

- •
  Architecture. Agents that each target one linguistic failure mode of
  monolithic models: fusion, compounding, and discourse ellipsis, rather
  than leaving all three to a single unguided generation call.
- •
  Empirical scale and significance. A pre-registered 12-condition
  ablation on $`N=1{,}000`$ verses (23,990 scored verdicts): full swarm
  beats the monolithic baseline by $`+0.63`$ MQM
  ($`p_{\text{adj}}=0.0018`$) and a call-count-matched self-refinement
  baseline by $`+0.51`$ MQM ($`p_{\text{adj}}=0.0288`$), via paired
  approximate randomization with Holm–Bonferroni correction and a
  measured noise floor rather than an uncorrected bootstrap-tail
  probability.
- •
  An isolated discourse-syntax finding. Ablating only the Ellipsis
  Restorer costs $`-0.44`$ MQM ($`p_{\text{adj}}=0.0288`$), representing
  the single largest individually-significant component effect, and the
  clearest evidence that a linguistically-motivated discourse module,
  not scale or generic self-critique, is doing the work.
- •
  Evaluation and decontamination rigor. We directly quantify LLM-judge
  self-preference ($`J_{\text{route}}`$ scores its own family’s outputs
  $`2`$–$`7`$ MQM higher than $`J_{\text{report}}`$ on every condition,
  which is why only $`J_{\text{report}}`$ is reported) and screen a
  192,151-entry retrieval index for reference leakage (0 leaks / 269
  runtime checks).

## 2 Related Work

#### Sanskrit Computational Linguistics

Prior work builds on foundational lexical-database and
morphological-analysis resources ([Huet, 2004](#bib.bib19)), and more
recently on neural sequence-to-sequence splitters ([Dave et al.,
2021](#bib.bib3)) and transformer tokenizers such as TransLIST ([Sandhan
et al., 2022](#bib.bib2)), integrated into tools like SanskritShala
([Sandhan et al., 2023](#bib.bib1)) and corpora such as the Digital
Corpus of Sanskrit ([Hellwig, 2010](#bib.bib20)).

#### LLMs for Machine Translation

General-purpose LLMs excel on high-resource languages ([Hendy et al.,
2023](#bib.bib25)) but struggle where parallel data is scarce ([Haddow
et al., 2022](#bib.bib12)). Two-stage fine-tuning, monolingual
pretraining followed by a small amount of high-quality parallel data
(ALMA, [Xu et al., 2024](#bib.bib13)), motivates our domain-aligned
gemma-2-mitra-it backbone ([Anonymous, 2026a](#bib.bib27)); scaling
efforts like NLLB-200 ([Costa-jussà et al., 2022](#bib.bib15)) expand
coverage without addressing classical-language-specific needs like
zero-anaphora resolution ([Wang et al., 2023](#bib.bib14)).

#### Multi-Agent Systems and Self-Refinement

Multi-agent debate among independent LLM instances improves factuality
and reasoning ([Du et al., 2023](#bib.bib24)); TransAgents ([Wu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib4)) showed multi-role literary translation with
specialized agents preferred by humans despite lower n-gram scores.
Self-refinement ([Madaan et al., 2023](#bib.bib5)) is directly
implemented, call-count-matched, as our self_refine ablation.
Tool-augmented reasoning ([Yao et al., 2023](#bib.bib6); [Schick et al.,
2023](#bib.bib7)) and retrieval augmentation ([Khandelwal et al.,
2021](#bib.bib18)) motivate
Section [3.6](#S3.SS6 "3.6 Agentic Feedback and Tool Retrieval ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation"),
where we report what happens when tool-use is restricted to tools
actually backed by data.

#### Reference-Free Evaluation and Judge Reliability

Reference-based metrics have documented validity limits ([Reiter,
2018](#bib.bib11)); reference-free QE ([Rei et al., 2022](#bib.bib17))
and fine-grained error-span detection ([Guerreiro et al.,
2024](#bib.bib16)) address this, as do LLM-as-judge frameworks ([Kocmi
and Federmann, 2023b](#bib.bib8); [Kocmi and Federmann,
2023a](#bib.bib9)) aided by chain-of-thought prompting ([Wei et al.,
2022](#bib.bib22)). Such judges also exhibit documented biases like
self-preference ([Zheng et al., 2023](#bib.bib10)): a judge sharing a
model family with the system it evaluates is one instance, and
Section [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Judge Validation: Self-Preference and Score-Arithmetic Reliability ‣ 5 Results and Analysis ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation")
measures it directly rather than assuming it away.

## 3 Methodology

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 1: System architecture of the MITRA-Swarm pipeline.
$`J_{\text{route}}`$ (same model family as the generators) drives the
internal critique loop; $`J_{\text{report}}`$ (independent vendor,
gpt-4o-mini) scores the finished output exactly once, off the critical
path, and is the only judge whose scores are reported as results
(Section [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Judge Validation: Self-Preference and Score-Arithmetic Reliability ‣ 5 Results and Analysis ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation")).

The MITRA-Swarm pipeline decomposes translation into chunking,
morphosemantic preprocessing, parallel drafting, discourse-aware
argument restoration, automated quality routing, and agentic refinement,
illustrated in
Figure [1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation")
and detailed with exact prompts in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Agent System Prompts and Prompt Templates ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation").

### 3.1 Document Segmentation (Chunking)

To manage context-window limits and preserve local discourse cohesion
([Liu et al., 2024](#bib.bib23)), the source document is segmented at
classical sentence/verse terminators (daṇḍa \|, dvipada daṇḍa \|\|), a
sliding token window ($`W=200`$, overlap $`O=40`$) for unpunctuated
prose, or an LLM-driven semantic chunker for narrative boundaries.

### 3.2 Morphological Pre-processing (Sandhi Parser)

A Sandhi Parser Agent decomposes phonetic mergers and compounds (Samāsa;
[Dave et al., 2021](#bib.bib3); [Sandhan et al., 2022](#bib.bib2)) into
a structured morphosemantic guide, threaded through a typed
TranslationRequest into every downstream translator call.
gemma-4-26B-A4B-it accepts the guide via its chat template;
gemma-2-mitra-it uses a legacy completion-style prompt for which guide
injection was evaluated empirically and disabled, so the
guide_only/guide_ellipsis contrasts reflect that per-model choice rather
than a uniform assumption.

### 3.3 Parallel Translation Array

The chunk is translated concurrently by a parallel array of models,

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathbf{T}=\{t_{\text{specialized}},t_{\text{frontier}},\dots\},
``` |  | (1) |

comprising the domain-specialized gemma-2-mitra-it ([Anonymous,
2026a](#bib.bib27)) and the generalist frontier gemma-4-26B-A4B-it
([Google, 2026](#bib.bib28)), both served locally via vLLM. Each model
generates a draft translation independently, and the routing judge
selects among candidates.

### 3.4 Ellipsis and Zero-Anaphora Argument Restoration with Register-Aware Voice Guarding

The Ellipsis Restorer operates over a sliding discourse window of the
preceding/succeeding chunks,
$`\mathbf{C}_{\text{discourse}}=\{c_{i-k},\dots,c_{i}\}`$, identifying
zero-anaphora and interpolating the implied argument. Naively restoring
an elided subject risks inventing a third-person actor in passages that
are impersonal or injunctive by design, where restoration could convert
a Dharmaśāstra injunction into an active clause with a hallucinated
subject. MITRA-Swarm mitigates this with a voice-preservation guard:
every source work ID is mapped, via a corpus-derived, manually verified
register table (registers.json; six registers (vedic, epic, legal,
sutra, kavya, shastra), covering over 100% of the corpus’s 52 work IDs,
rather than inferred from a keyword heuristic), to a voice_preserving
flag. Legal and sutra are flagged voice-preserving as characteristically
impersonal/passive by genre; the Ellipsis Restorer receives the literal
genre hint "legal" for any work so flagged, and the raw register name
otherwise, which measurably changes its restoration behavior
(Section [A](#A1 "Appendix A Qualitative Analysis: Register-Aware Voice Preservation ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation"))
without a separate model or prompt per register.

### 3.5 Two-Judge Quality Architecture

Quality estimation is split into two roles, enforced at startup by an
automated model-family check. $`J_{\text{route}}`$ (Routing Judge): a
locally-hosted gemma-4-26B-A4B-it instance, sharing a model family with
the generators, scores intermediate drafts $`S_{j}\in[0,100]`$ against
threshold $`T_{\text{judge}}=80`$ to decide whether the critique loop
fires; because it shares a family with what it evaluates and is queried
repeatedly during generation, its scores are an internal control signal
only, never reported as a result. $`J_{\text{report}}`$ (Reporting
Judge): an independent offline judge (openai:gpt-4o-mini), sharing no
vendor lineage with either generator or $`J_{\text{route}}`$, invoked
exactly once per finished output on a separate machine from the
generation cluster. Every number in
Section [5](#S5 "5 Results and Analysis ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation")
is a $`J_{\text{report}}`$ score.

Both judges use a GEMBA-style rubric returning structured error spans
(category, severity, verbatim span, explanation) rather than a bare
number. The headline MQM is *recomputed* deterministically from that
list using fixed severity weights (critical $`=-25`$, major $`=-5`$,
minor $`=-1`$, floored at 0), not the model’s own top-line arithmetic,
which is retained separately for the judge-validation diagnostic
(Section [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Judge Validation: Self-Preference and Score-Arithmetic Reliability ‣ 5 Results and Analysis ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation")).
A failed judge call yields a missing score, excluded from all
aggregates, rather than a sentinel $`0.0`$ that would otherwise depress
the mean and minimum and spuriously trigger the critique loop.

### 3.6 Agentic Feedback and Tool Retrieval

If $`S_{j}<T_{\text{judge}}`$, a Critique Agent diagnoses errors, a Tool
Selector queries whichever tools are genuinely backed by data, and a
Refinement Agent synthesizes the draft, critique, and retrieved context
into a revised translation, re-scored up to $`M`$ iterations. The
inventory is reported *as offered*: a tool with no backing index is
absent rather than present and silently returning a canned string. On
the air-gapped GH200 cluster used here, that inventory reduces to
TRANSLATION_MEMORY, which performs fuzzy character-6-gram matching
against a decontaminated corpus index
(Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Data Decontamination and Preflight Reference-Echo Screening ‣ 4 Experimental Setup ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation")).
A DICTIONARY tool (offline lexicon lookup, with entries OCR-sanitized to
strip 19th-century scanning artifacts before reaching the Refinement
Agent) exists but was not backed by a snapshot in this run; ALIGNMENT
and live SEARCH require, respectively, an alignment index and network
access unavailable offline. A Dedup Agent stitches overlapping segments
pairwise, $`t_{\text{merged}}=\text{Stitch}(t_{i-1},t_{i})`$, feeding
only the tail of the running translation (last $`L=600`$ characters) so
per-step input stays bounded rather than growing with the number of
merged segments.

## 4 Experimental Setup

### 4.1 Evaluation Dataset and Stratification

Experiments are conducted on a stratified sample of $`N=1{,}000`$ verses
drawn, proportionally by register, from the 5,552-verse test partition
(12 works) of the MitraSamgraha corpus ([Anonymous, 2026b](#bib.bib26)).
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Evaluation Dataset and Stratification ‣ 4 Experimental Setup ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation")
reports the realised sample against the full test-partition population
for each of the five registers represented in this partition; the
register-to-work-ID mapping is manually verified (100% work-ID coverage,
0 unmapped) rather than inferred from a keyword heuristic.

| Register |  Description                      | Pop.  | Sample | Voice-preserv. |
|----------|-----------------------------------|-------|--------|----------------|
| epic     |  Itihāsa/Purāṇa narrative         | 1,720 | 310    | –              |
| sutra    |  Philosophical sūtra, commentary  | 1,488 | 268    | ✓              |
| vedic    |  Vedic saṃhitā/upaniṣad; archaic  | 1,000 | 180    | –              |
| kavya    |  Ornate metrical poetry           | 844   | 152    | –              |
| legal    |  Dharmaśāstra, nibandha           | 500   | 90     | ✓              |
| Total    |                                   | 5,552 | 1,000  |                |

Table 1: Register composition of the $`N=1{,}000`$ evaluation sample,
proportional to its population in the 5,552-verse test partition.
Voice-preserving marks registers routed to the impersonal-voice guard in
the Ellipsis Restorer
(Section [3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Ellipsis and Zero-Anaphora Argument Restoration with Register-Aware Voice Guarding ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation")).

This sample size balances statistical power with the cost of a
12-condition ablation (12,000 full pipeline runs). Because the corpus is
drawn from 12 works with substantial internal stylistic variation,
register-level results are an average over that variation, not a claim
of uniformity within it.

### 4.2 Data Decontamination and Preflight Reference-Echo Screening

To ensure rigorous evaluation and prevent data leakage, the
TRANSLATION_MEMORY index contains $`192{,}151`$ segment-level entries,
with all 12 evaluation work IDs excluded at build time ($`125{,}665`$
entries excluded; $`0`$ evaluation work IDs reachable in the live
index). A runtime reference-echo detector computes character 6-gram
F-score similarity between every retrieved string and the gold reference
that triggered it, flagging anything $`\geq 0.6`$; across a 200-item
preflight check and 269 runtime retrievals, the maximum observed
similarity is $`0.375`$, with $`0`$ echoes flagged. We separately audit
translator outputs against the gold reference for suspected
training-data memorization (independent of retrieval): $`0.21\%`$ of
gemma and $`0.70\%`$ of mitra outputs exceed a $`0.6`$ "suspect"
threshold, with $`0.15\%`$ of mitra outputs exceeding a stricter $`0.8`$
threshold; inspection shows short sentences (e.g., "He makes offering(s)
to four deities") with only a one-word paraphrase gap, not
retrieval-time leakage.

### 4.3 Models and Hardware

The generator array comprises gemma-4-26B-A4B-it (26B-parameter MoE, 4B
active) and gemma-2-mitra-it, both served locally via vLLM on NVIDIA
GH200 nodes; $`J_{\text{route}}`$ runs on the same endpoint.
$`J_{\text{report}}`$ runs offline, after generation, against the OpenAI
API (gpt-4o-mini), since the generation cluster is air-gapped.

### 4.4 Hyperparameters and Compute Budget

Translation agents decode at temperature $`0.0`$;
critique/judge/tool-selector agents at $`0.1`$; serving context window
is capped at $`4{,}096`$ tokens (with a $`2{,}048`$-token output cap) to
optimize batch throughput across verse segments, well within the models’
native context windows.
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.4 Hyperparameters and Compute Budget ‣ 4 Experimental Setup ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation")
compares per-verse token budget and latency for the three conditions
central to the main results (full per-condition table in Appendix
Table [10](#A2.T10 "Table 10 ‣ Appendix B Supplementary Tables ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation")),
measured directly from run instrumentation, not estimated. Across the
full run, generation consumed $`17.61`$M tokens ($`10.71`$M prompt,
$`6.90`$M completion) across $`85{,}509`$ LLM calls at a $`54.9\%`$
cache hit rate; the routing judge alone accounts for $`17{,}713`$ calls
($`12.57`$M tokens), since $`J_{\text{route}}`$ is queried once per
candidate per stage rather than once per verse.

| Configuration | Prompt tok. | Compl. tok. | Total/verse | Latency (s) |
|---------------|-------------|-------------|-------------|-------------|
| baseline      | 91          | 49          | 140         | 2.5         |
| self_refine   | 164         | 89          | 253         | 4.9         |
| bo_n          | 455         | 258         | 713         | 12.8        |
| full_swarm    | 828         | 462         | 1290        | 7.1         |

Table 2: Per-verse compute, key conditions (measured, not estimated).
Full swarm costs $`9.2\times`$ baseline tokens for $`+0.63`$ MQM.

### 4.5 Ablation Matrix

We pre-register a 12-condition ablation matrix (full active-component
flags in Appendix
Table [8](#A2.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix B Supplementary Tables ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation")),
isolating each architectural component against a monolithic baseline, a
paired test-retest control, a placebo re-judging control, and two
compute-matched controls (best-of-$`N`$ and generic self-refinement):
baseline (monolithic single-pass, no guide/ellipsis/loop); baseline_dup
(different seed; the noise floor); placebo_rejudge (baseline re-judged;
judge-side noise only); bo_n (compute-matched best-of-5, temperature
0.7); self_refine (call-count-matched generic self-critique, no role
specialization); guide_only (Sandhi guide alone); guide_ellipsis
(guide + Ellipsis Restorer, no loop/tools); no_guide, no_ellipsis (the
isolated discourse-restoration ablation), no_critique, no_tools (full
swarm minus one component each); and full_swarm, the complete
architecture
(Section [3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Ellipsis and Zero-Anaphora Argument Restoration with Register-Aware Voice Guarding ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation")–[3.6](#S3.SS6 "3.6 Agentic Feedback and Tool Retrieval ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation")).

### 4.6 Metrics and Statistical Plan

Quality is MQM, a reference-free $`[0,100]`$ score from
$`J_{\text{report}}`$
(Section [3.5](#S3.SS5 "3.5 Two-Judge Quality Architecture ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation")).
Significance uses a paired approximate randomization test ([Riezler and
Maxwell, 2005](#bib.bib29), the standard for MT system comparison rather
than a bootstrap-tail probability;) at $`R=10{,}000`$, with 95% BCa
bootstrap CIs ($`B=10{,}000`$); all 10 pre-registered contrasts are
corrected jointly with Holm–Bonferroni. Because mean MQM is compressed
near 85–86 for every condition, we also report a measured noise floor:
the mean absolute difference between baseline and baseline_dup is
$`0.21`$ MQM, and a contrast is *reportable* only if it is both
significant *and* exceeds this floor; a significant result smaller than
the chance disagreement between two identical systems is a measurement
of the harness, not the method.

Four trends are reportable under the criterion in
Section [4.6](#S4.SS6 "4.6 Metrics and Statistical Plan ‣ 4 Experimental Setup ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation")
(significant and above the noise floor). (1) The full swarm beats the
monolithic baseline by $`+0.63`$ MQM ($`p_{\text{adj}}=0.0018`$, CI
$`[+0.30,+0.97]`$, $`d_{z}=0.12`$, 397/294/308 W/L/T), which is real but
small in absolute terms (both means sit at 85.3–85.9 of 100), which we
report plainly. (2) Removing only the Ellipsis Restorer costs $`-0.44`$
MQM relative to the full swarm ($`p_{\text{adj}}=0.0288`$,
$`[+0.12,+0.73]`$, 323/232/444 W/L/T), constituting the single largest
individually-significant component effect, confirming that discourse
restoration operates effectively in isolation. (3) The swarm beats a
call-count-matched generic self-refinement baseline by $`+0.51`$ MQM
($`p_{\text{adj}}=0.0288`$, 389/301/309 W/L/T), attributable to role
specialization and discourse/morphology structure rather than extra
inference calls alone. (4) Adding the Ellipsis Restorer on top of the
Sandhi guide alone yields $`+0.69`$ MQM ($`p_{\text{adj}}=0.001`$,
$`[+0.39,+1.00]`$, $`d_{z}=0.14`$), the largest effect size in the
matrix, consistent with (2).

The other six contrasts are *not* reportable, and a null from a
well-controlled comparison is itself informative: the Sandhi guide
alone, against the full swarm ($`-0.01`$) or the baseline ($`-0.04`$,
guide_only); the critique loop in isolation ($`-0.02`$); tool retrieval
($`+0.01`$;
Section [3.6](#S3.SS6 "3.6 Agentic Feedback and Tool Retrieval ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation")
explains why, given the tool inventory actually available); the placebo
re-judging control ($`-0.01`$, confirming judge stability under repeat
scoring); and full swarm vs. best-of-$`N`$ ($`+0.32`$,
$`p_{\text{adj}}=0.460`$, numerically positive and above the floor but
not significant, though a large enough compute-matched sampling budget
may close some of this gap).

These findings replicate under a fully deterministic, reference-based
metric. To check they do not depend on a single judge’s preferences, we
additionally compute chrF++ ([Popović, 2017](#bib.bib30)) via sacrebleu
(word order 2) over the same selected outputs. The full swarm’s
advantage over baseline holds under this judge-independent metric
($`29.27\to 30.33`$ chrF++, $`p_{\text{adj}}=0.0010`$), as does isolated
ellipsis restoration ($`+0.73`$, $`p_{\text{adj}}=0.0010`$) and the gain
over self-refine ($`+0.78`$, $`p_{\text{adj}}=0.0010`$); the same
noise-floor check that gates the MQM contrasts flags marginal
seed-to-seed chrF variance on its own ($`p=0.033`$), smaller than the
reported effects but disclosed rather than omitted.

Restricting to baseline, the isolated ellipsis ablation, and the full
swarm (full 12-condition breakdown in Appendix
Table [9](#A2.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Appendix B Supplementary Tables ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation")),
the full-swarm gain over baseline is largest in vedic ($`83.6\to 84.5`$,
$`+0.9`$; heaviest ellipsis, most archaic morphology), moderate in kavya
($`+0.4`$), legal, and sutra ($`+0.3`$ each), and flat in epic
($`+0.0`$). This pattern is consistent with, though not definitive proof
of, the discourse-restoration mechanism in
Section [3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Ellipsis and Zero-Anaphora Argument Restoration with Register-Aware Voice Guarding ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation"):
the voice-preserving registers (legal, sutra) do not show the largest
numeric gains, since the voice guard changes *how* arguments are
restored
(Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Qualitative Analysis: Register-Aware Voice Preservation ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation"))
rather than guaranteeing the largest score delta.

Error-category counts (mean per segment by MQM category, Appendix
Table [11](#A2.T11 "Table 11 ‣ Appendix B Supplementary Tables ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation"))
are dominated by mistranslation and omission in every condition; the
full swarm shows a modest omission reduction relative to
no_ellipsis/baseline, alongside a small rise in flagged mistranslation
spans, since the critique loop rewrites text and not every rewrite is
judged an improvement. The tail of the per-verse score distribution
(Appendix
Figure [2](#A2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Appendix B Supplementary Tables ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation"))
confirms the system’s effect is concentrated in the low tail (P10,
minimum, %$`<80`$ in
Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.1 Main Ablation Results ‣ 5 Results and Analysis ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation"))
rather than a uniform shift of the whole distribution, since the mean is
compressed near 85–86 for every condition.

### 5.2 Judge Validation: Self-Preference and Score-Arithmetic Reliability

Table [5](#S5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 5.2 Judge Validation: Self-Preference and Score-Arithmetic Reliability ‣ 5 Results and Analysis ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation")
summarizes the evaluation-methodology findings motivating the two-judge
split (full per-condition self-preference in Appendix
Table [12](#A2.T12 "Table 12 ‣ Appendix B Supplementary Tables ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation")).
Self-preference is large and universal: on every one of the 12
conditions, $`J_{\text{route}}`$ scores the output $`1.9`$–$`6.8`$ MQM
higher than $`J_{\text{report}}`$. Reporting $`J_{\text{route}}`$’s own
scores, as a single-judge design would, would inflate every headline
number by an amount that itself varies by condition, biasing
cross-condition comparison; to our knowledge, this is one of the more
direct in-pipeline measurements of LLM-judge self-preference reported
for a low-resource MT system. The judge’s own arithmetic disagrees with
its stated rubric on $`96.4\%`$ of scored items (mean $`|\Delta|=16.37`$
between the self-reported score and the score recomputed from its own
error spans), which is why we report the recomputed score as the metric
and both scores as a diagnostic. Recomputing MQM is a deliberate
departure from the published GEMBA-MQM protocol, so the two are not
numerically interchangeable with prior work using the standard prompt.
Test-retest reliability has a within-item SD of $`1.45`$ MQM, smaller
than the smallest reportable effect in
Table [4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 5.1 Main Ablation Results ‣ 5 Results and Analysis ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation");
the reporting judge’s failure rate is $`0.41\%`$.

Few-shot prompting reduces, but does not eliminate, this arithmetic gap.
Motivated by the concern that a zero-shot judge may simply be
miscalibrated, we re-score a stratified subsample, the same 100 items
per condition, paired across all twelve, with a three-shot variant of
the judge prompt. This reduces the arithmetic-disagreement rate from
$`96.4\%`$ to $`79.3\%`$ (mean $`|\Delta|`$: $`16.37\to 8.46`$) but
leaves most items still disagreeing, reinforcing that recomputing the
score from error spans is not an optional refinement. Zero-shot and
few-shot scores on the same items correlate only moderately (Pearson
$`r=0.47`$, Spearman $`\rho=0.60`$), indicating the judge’s output is
itself non-trivially prompt-sensitive. At $`n=100`$ per condition the
pre-registered contrasts do not reach significance here
($`n\approx 146`$ is needed to detect a 2-point effect), so we treat
this as a calibration diagnostic, not a second significance test.

| Judge diagnostic | Value |
|----|----|
| Reporting judge | openai:gpt-4o-mini |
| Judge failure rate | 0.41% |
| Arithmetic disagrees with rubric | 96.4% (mean $`|\Delta|`$ = 16.37) |
| Test–retest SD (repeated calls) | 1.45 |
| Self-preference range (min–max, 12 conditions) | +1.94 to +6.79 |

Table 5: Judge validation summary under the zero-shot judge prompt (the
few-shot comparison above is a separate, $`n=100`$-per-condition
subsample). Self-preference range is
$`J_{\text{route}}-J_{\text{report}}`$ over the 12 conditions.

### 5.3 Tool Utility

Table [6](#S5.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 5.3 Tool Utility ‣ 5 Results and Analysis ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation")
reports usage for the TRANSLATION_MEMORY tool: 5,513 queries, $`4.9\%`$
hit rate, zero transport errors. Its measured effect ($`+0.01`$ MQM,
Table [4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 5.1 Main Ablation Results ‣ 5 Results and Analysis ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation"))
is below the noise floor, representing a genuine negative result rather
than an artifact: fuzzy translation-memory lookup rarely finds a close
precedent for an unseen verse, and when it does, the 26B-parameter
generalist model already appears to carry comparable lexical knowledge
parametrically.

## 6 Conclusion

We introduced MITRA-Swarm, a multi-agent architecture injecting explicit
linguistic structure (Sandhi splitting, register-aware discourse
ellipsis restoration, and a two-judge quality architecture) into an
otherwise monolithic foundation-model pipeline for classical Sanskrit.
On a pre-registered, stratified $`N=1{,}000`$ benchmark, the swarm
produces small but statistically robust gains over a monolithic baseline
and a call-count-matched self-refinement baseline, with the isolated
discourse-restoration ablation as the single largest component effect.
Equally central is what the benchmark says about evaluation itself:
LLM-judge self-preference is large and universal (2–7 MQM, every
condition), and a preflight decontamination sweep is directly
falsifiable and, here, clean. A foundation-model system for a
morphologically rich, low-resource classical language should be
evaluated with rigorous self-scrutiny; we release the pipeline, matrix,
and diagnostics so that findings can be independently reproduced. Future
work: gold linguistic annotation to measure each agent against the
phenomenon it targets rather than only aggregate MQM; extension to
Classical Tibetan and Pāli; and a multi-judge reporting panel to bound
the single-judge design’s residual uncertainty.

## Limitations

- •
  Effects are small relative to the metric’s range. Every condition
  scores 85.2–85.9 of 100; the effect concentrates in the low tail, not
  a uniform mean shift, and should not be extrapolated to a metric with
  more headroom.
- •
  A single reporting judge is a single point of failure. Despite the
  validation in
  Section [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Judge Validation: Self-Preference and Score-Arithmetic Reliability ‣ 5 Results and Analysis ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation"),
  the headline metric rests on one model; a multi-judge panel (future
  work) would strengthen this.
- •
  The noise floor bounds generation variance, not judge variance, since
  baseline/baseline_dup differ only in seed and are judged at
  temperature 0 with caching.
- •
  Recomputing MQM from error spans departs from the published GEMBA-MQM
  protocol (96.4% disagreement with the model’s own arithmetic,
  Section [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Judge Validation: Self-Preference and Score-Arithmetic Reliability ‣ 5 Results and Analysis ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation")),
  so it is not numerically comparable to prior work reporting the raw
  score.
- •
  bo_n decodes at temperature 0.7 vs. 0.0 for every other condition:
  this is inherent to best-of-$`N`$, but a genuine confound.
- •
  Single-prompt reasoning baselines: While self_refine and bo_n provide
  compute-matched controls, exploring unified single-prompt
  Chain-of-Thought reasoning (prompting a single frontier model to
  perform Sandhi analysis and discourse tracking in explicit scratchpad
  tokens before emitting a translation) represents a valuable direction
  for future baseline comparisons.
- •
  Ensemble aggregation vs. routing: The parallel drafting array selects
  the top candidate via $`J_{\text{route}}`$; evaluating multi-candidate
  synthesis/aggregation models rather than tournament routing remains an
  open architectural alternative.

#### Ethical considerations.

Multi-agent inference raises compute cost per query relative to
single-pass models
(Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.4 Hyperparameters and Compute Budget ‣ 4 Experimental Setup ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation")),
acceptable for offline research but warranting caching and
hardware-efficiency care before deployment; translating culturally and
religiously loaded terminology (Dharma, Śūnya) risks interpretive drift,
which the voice guard and independent evaluation aim to mitigate. We
credit and respect the licenses of the open assets used: MitraSamgraha
(CC-BY-SA 4.0; [Anonymous, 2026b](#bib.bib26)) and the Gemma model
family (Gemma Open License; [Google, 2026](#bib.bib28)).

## Appendix A Qualitative Analysis: Register-Aware Voice Preservation

Table [7](#A1.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Appendix A Qualitative Analysis: Register-Aware Voice Preservation ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation")
shows an unedited pipeline output pair for a legal (Manusmṛti,
voice-preserving) verse. Both conditions produce fluent, accurate
English; the full swarm’s Ellipsis Restorer, informed that this work is
voice-preserving, rewrites the target clause as an impersonal passive
("the mind should be turned away…") rather than an invented active
third-person subject ("one should turn the mind away…"), matching the
impersonal register rather than converting it to a personal directive.
We report this as a mechanism demonstration, not a large per-item MQM
swing: per-item routing-judge scores are a diagnostic signal, not a
reported metric
(Section [3.5](#S3.SS5 "3.5 Two-Judge Quality Architecture ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation"));
the statistically assessed effect of this mechanism is the
register-stratified pattern
(Section [5](#S5 "5 Results and Analysis ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation"))
and the isolated ablation
(Section [5](#S5 "5 Results and Analysis ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation"),
trend 2), not any single verse.

| Source |  indriyārtheṣu sarveṣu na prasajyeta kāmataḥ / atiprasaktiṃ caiteṣāṃ manasā saṃnivartayet // |
|----|----|
| Gold Reference |  “…let him carefully obviate an excessive attachment to them, by (reflecting on their worthlessness in) his heart.” |
| no_ellipsis (guard inactive) |  “…furthermore, one should turn the mind away from excessive attachment to these.” |
| full_swarm (legal $`\to`$ passive) |  “…furthermore, the mind should be turned away from excessive attachment to these.” |

Table 7: Register-aware voice preservation, an unedited output pair
(Manusmṛti 2.98, item GSD36manu_test:130).

## Appendix C Agent System Prompts and Prompt Templates

In this appendix, we provide the exact system instructions, prompt
templates, and JSON schemas used by the various subagents in MITRA-Swarm
to ensure full reproducibility of the agentic behaviors.

### C.1 Morphological Pre-processing (Sandhi Parser Agent)

The Sandhi Parser Agent is responsible for decomposing complex phonetic
mergers and nominal compounds before translation begins. Its output is
threaded into every downstream translator call via a typed
TranslationRequest.guide field (Section 3.2).

``` ltx_verbatim
System Instruction:
You are an expert Sanskrit grammarian.
Analyze the input Sanskrit text. Identify
complex compound words (Samasa) and
phonetic joins (Sandhi). Write down the
compound word splits and explain the
individual components briefly to assist a
translator. Format your output as a concise
split analysis. If there are no complex
compounds, reply: ’No complex compounds.’

Prompt Template:
Analyze compounds/sandhi in this text:

{source_chunk}
````

### C.2 Discourse Argument Restoration (Ellipsis Restorer Agent)

This agent operates over a sliding window to interpolate omitted
arguments (zero-anaphora) into the draft translation. In production, the
genre field passed below is "legal" whenever the source work ID is
flagged voice_preserving in the register table (covering the legal and
sutra registers), and the literal register name otherwise
(Section [3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Ellipsis and Zero-Anaphora Argument Restoration with Register-Aware Voice Guarding ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation")).

```ltx_verbatim
System Instruction:
You are an expert classical language editor.
Sanskrit frequently omits pronouns,
subjects, or verbs (ellipses) when they are
clear from context. Review the source
Sanskrit text, the surrounding discourse
context, and the draft English translation.
If the source genre is impersonal or
injunctive (e.g. legal/sutra), prefer
impersonal or passive restorations over
inventing an active third-person subject.
Identify if any implied arguments are
missing in the draft English translation. If
so, write down the restored/improved
translation. If the draft translation is
already complete, accurate, and fluent,
return the draft translation EXACTLY as is.
Return only the final English text without
explanations or headers.

Prompt Template:
Source Sanskrit:
{source}

Source genre: {genre}

Draft English Translation:
{draft_translation}

Surrounding Discourse Context:
  - Preceding Chunk: {prev_chunk}
  - Succeeding Chunk: {next_chunk}

Output the restored translation:
```

### C.3 Quality Evaluation Judge (GEMBA-MQM)

Both $`J_{\text{route}}`$ and $`J_{\text{report}}`$
(Section [3.5](#S3.SS5 "3.5 Two-Judge Quality Architecture ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation"))
use this prompt; the reported metric is the deterministic score
recomputed from errors using the fixed weights below, not the model’s
own top-line number, which is retained separately as
model_reported_score for the judge-validation diagnostic in
Section [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Judge Validation: Self-Preference and Score-Arithmetic Reliability ‣ 5 Results and Analysis ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation").

```ltx_verbatim
System Instruction:
You are an expert translation quality evaluator
trained in MQM (Multidimensional Quality
Metrics). You identify translation errors from
classical languages into English and assign
severity levels. Be rigorous but fair. Respond
strictly in the JSON schema requested.

Prompt Template:
Source language: {lang_name}
Source text:
"""
{source}
"""

Candidate translation (English):
"""
{translation}
"""

Identify every translation error. For each,
choose:
  - category: one of [accuracy/mistranslation,
    accuracy/omission, accuracy/addition,
    accuracy/untranslated, fluency/grammar,
    fluency/register, fluency/spelling,
    fluency/punctuation, style/awkward,
    terminology, other]
  - severity: one of [minor, major, critical]
  - span: the offending English substring
    (verbatim)
  - explanation: one short sentence

Then compute an overall MQM score. Use the standard weights:
  critical = -25, major = -5, minor = -1
  score = max(0, 100 + sum(weights))

Return ONLY valid JSON matching:
{
  "errors": [
    {"category": "...", "severity": "...", "span": "...",
     "explanation": "..."}
  ],
  "score": <number 0-100>,
  "rationale": "<one sentence summary>"
}
```

### C.4 Critique and Tool-Selector Agents

When a translation falls below the quality threshold, the Critique Agent
diagnoses the errors, and the Tool Selector Agent retrieves necessary
context strictly from the tools reported as available in the current
environment
(Section [3.6](#S3.SS6 "3.6 Agentic Feedback and Tool Retrieval ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation"));
for the benchmark in this paper, that inventory reduces to
TRANSLATION_MEMORY.

```ltx_verbatim
Critique Agent System Instruction:
You are a senior translation editor. A Sanskrit-to-English translation
has received a low evaluation score from our automated judge. Perform a
detailed critique. Identify errors, mistranslations, omissions, or
terminology mismatches in the draft compared to the Sanskrit source.
Suggest specific corrections.

Tool Selector Agent System Instruction:
You are a research coordinator routing translation tasks to tools. Review
the Sanskrit source text and the critique. Determine which tools from
the inventory below are needed to resolve the issues. Only tools listed
here are available in this environment; do not request any other tool.
Available Tools (environment-reported; varies by run):
1. TRANSLATION_MEMORY: fuzzy-match the source against a decontaminated
   parallel corpus for sentence-level precedents (query = Sanskrit text).
2. DICTIONARY: look up a headword in the offline lexicon snapshot, if
   one is configured for this run (query = single word in IAST).
3. ALIGNMENT: Tibetan/Classical Chinese parallel alignment, if an
   alignment index is configured for this run (query = Sanskrit keyword).

You must select between 0 and 3 tool calls. Return your selection ONLY
as a JSON list of dictionaries, e.g.:
[
  {"tool": "TRANSLATION_MEMORY", "query": "citraśravaḥ tama havante"}
]
Do not output markdown code blocks or any
explanation.
```
